curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: Unnamed `""`; yank `"0`; numbered `"1`–`"9`; named `"a`–`"z`; append with `"A`–`"Z`; black-hole `"_`; small delete `"-`; clipboard `"+`; read-only `".` `":` `"/`; `p P gp gP`; `:registers` as inspection; command-line `Ctrl-r{register}`; Insert-mode `Ctrl-r{register}`
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Preserve yanks, select storage deliberately, reuse multiple snippets, understand why delete/change affects later puts, and read back what Vim already recorded instead of retyping it
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Delete without overwriting a yank; paste the previous yank after another edit; collect lines into a named register; reuse a confirmed search pattern in a substitution; choose where to put text and where the cursor should land
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core through named, black-hole, and read-only registers. The useful but host-dependent `"+` clipboard is emulated inside each Vim Wilds exercise and never touches the device clipboard. Numbered recovery, small-delete recovery, and `gp`/`gP` stay on the path marked advanced rather than removed. Insert-mode `Ctrl-r` is native Vim; a host editor that embeds Vim may claim that Ctrl chord by default, so check the host you are in

lessons.title: Understand the unnamed register
lessons.objective: See how yank, delete, and change feed the default register used by an unprefixed put.

activities.title: Vim saves copied and deleted text
activities.body: Yank, delete, and change commands save text in the unnamed register. Plain `p` and `P` use its latest value, so a newer edit can replace what you planned to put.
activities.grammar: operator → unnamed register → p or P
activities.contrast: The explicit name is `""`, but ordinary puts use it automatically.

activities.title: Numbered registers keep large deletes

activities.contrast: Numbered history is newest-first; it is not the same as yank register zero.

lessons.title: Recover small deletes
lessons.objective: Retrieve the latest deletion or change that was shorter than a line.
lessons.trackNote: Advanced and less commonly used: `u` undoes a small delete faster than `"-p` restores it, but the register explains why a small delete never enters the numbered history.

activities.title: Small deletes have their own register
activities.body: A delete or change shorter than one line is saved in register `-` rather than in the numbered history. Only the most recent one is kept.
activities.grammar: less than a line → "- · a whole line → "1
activities.contrast: Numbered registers collect whole lines; the small-delete register collects everything shorter.

activities.title: Registers reach into Insert mode
activities.body: `Ctrl-r` followed by a register name types that register's contents at the cursor and leaves you in Insert mode. It reads the register without changing it, so the same value is still there for the next put. Every register works this way: `0` for the last yank, `"` for the unnamed register, a letter for a named one, and the read-only `.`, `:`, and `/` for what you last inserted, ran, and searched for. Some editors that embed Vim claim this chord for themselves, so check the host you are in.

reference.purpose: Read back the last inserted text, the last Ex command, and the last search pattern.
notes: Vim fills these; no command writes them directly.

reference.purpose: Insert a register's text into the command line instead of retyping it.
notes: `Ctrl-r/` reuses the pattern a search just confirmed.
Any readable register works, including named ones.
Register type controls whether a put is characterwise, linewise, or blockwise.

reference.purpose: Type a register's contents into the text you are inserting.
notes: Reads the register without changing it, and keeps the insert open.
"0 still holds the last yank after a delete has claimed the unnamed register.
The read-only ". ": and "/ registers work here too.
Some editors that embed Vim claim this chord for themselves; check the host you are in.
